speechtext:
The house resumed from Wednesday, March 13, consideration in committee of Bill No. 21, to provide for limiting the hours of work in industrial undertakings to eight in the day and forty-eight in the week, in accordance with the convention concerning the application of the principle of the eight hour day or of the forty-eight hour week adopted by the general conference of the international labour organization of the League of Nations,
(Mr. R. Weir.]
in accordance with the labour part of the treaty of Versailles of 28th June, 1019,-Mr. Gordon (for Mr. Bennett)-Mr. Morand in the chair.
P. F. CASGRAIN (Charlevoix-Saguenay): Mr. Chairman, I 'have in my hand a letter addressed to the hon. member for St. Hya-cinthe-Rouville (Mr. Fontaine) which I have been asked to read to the house in the absence of the hon.. member. This letter is in connection with the working hours in certain industries such as the canning industry. The letter is dated February 26, 1935, and reads as follows:
The convention applies to all industrial undertaking which of course includes all manufacturers. While we approve these regulations for the industry in general, on behalf of the canning industry we feel that certain provisions of these regulations would not work out satisfactorily in our industry, and would cause in some instances very serious hardship to the growers who are furnishing the raw products to our industry, as many factories are located in centres of a small population, and owing to the nature of our business whereas we may have heavy deliveries one day, and light deliveries another day, due to climatic or other conditions, we feel that it is pretty nearly impossible to secure sufficient help to work two shifts in these centres.
Also taking in consideration that all produce pertaining to a canning industry is perishable in a great many instances within few hours, therefore it is necessary that this produce be taken care of regardless to the hours we may have to do so, other than this it would be a total loss to the growers.
We also had instances where during the rush of the season the rain held farmers from harvesting their crop causing the factory _ to have to close up or work just few hours during that time, and was then necessary for the factory to work long hours to catch up again, or otherwise the grower would loose his crop. Owing to the fact that most canning factories are only a seasonal operation, we feel in this particular respect that there should be some special provisions to work hours necessary to handle farmers crops without any injury to the help.
We trust we have made ourselves plain and that you may see your way clear to take this matter belfore the house.
Respectfully yours,
St. Hyacinthe Canning Factory.
(Signed) J. H. Logan.
A letter enclosing a copy of this letter was sent to the Prime Minister. I put this letter on record so that these people will have their wish known to the house.

BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Section
10 is one to which a good deal of study has been given and we desire to make some amendments. In order to clarify them we have had a new section 10 drafted. I therefore beg to move that the section as at present printed in the bill be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
10.	(1) The governor in council may by
regulation except any or all employment in any industry from the limits of hours of work fixed by this act, whenever he is satisfied that,
(a)	the work of the employees must necessarily be carried on outside the limits laid down for the general working of an establishment because it is preparatory or complementary, or that,
(b)	the work is essentially intermittent in that,
(1)	the worker is not continuously occupied during the hours of employment, or
(ii)	the work is seasonal in its nature, or
(iii)	the work is of such a character that it must necessarily be performed in variable periods of employment, or
(iv)	the work in its nature is subject to intervals of discontinuance or variations in supply of raw materials, or that
(c)	there is an exceptional pressure of work;
Provided that fair and humane conditions of
labour in the matter of hours of work prevail in respect of such employment; and provided further that in the case of exceptional pressure of work the regulation shall be temporary.
(2)	If any organizations of employers and workers concerned in the employment affected by any regulation made under this section exist, such organizations shall be consulted.
(3)	Whenever it is practicable the maximum of additional hours shall be fixed by the regulations and in any such case the rate of pay for additional hours shall not be less than one and one-quarter times the regular rate.

subtopic: BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
I wonder if the minister would let this new section stand over. It is so long and complicated that it is utterly impossible for one to grasp its scope by hearing it read even a couple of times. As I have heard portions of it read, it may go a long way to meet some of the objections I have raised, but I should like the minister to let it stand. It says something about "where it is possible"; that is rather difficult to understand in regard to fixing the maximum of additional hours. What does "additional" mean? Suppose in the fishing industry they work four hours today and want to work twelve hours the next day so that you have the equivalent of the eight hour day. Does the word "additional", carrying time and a quarter, apply on the second day to all the hours in excess of eight, or would it only apply to all the hours over forty-eight in a week? It makes a substantial difference. Apparently the purport of the amendment is to equalize the hours. If they
have to work only a few hours to-day, owing to the fact that the fish are not coming in, they will work longer to-morrow. Now if the suggestion is that when they work four hours to-day and twelve the next day, under these circumstances, all the hours beyond eight on the second day must be paid for as time and a quarter, then there will be a hardship not only on those who are running the plant but also on the employees, because there will be a tendency for the plant on the second day to say, "We will not work over eight hours to-day because it will be too costly", and they might simply refuse to take the fish, with the result that men who have gone out on their own to get the fish will not be able to sell them.

If they worked four hours to-day and twelve hours to-morrow the time and a quarter would not apply.

I do not think the hon.
gentleman need be worried about the des-

truction of the bill because of this amendment. The proposed amendments are designed to enable the governor in council by regulation to exempt in any industry such activities as cannot be strictly adjusted to the eight hour principle. I did not say that it
would; I said that it might. The wording is very strong; it is to the effect that the governor in council may by regulation exempt any and all occupations from the effects of the eight hour day bill. The point I wish to raise is that the workers in the industry, for whom this legislation is ostensibly put on the statute books, have no say in its organization or management, or in the way in which it works. Consequently the employers may say that such and such is not feasible or possible; yet if an effort is made in conjunction with the employees by bringing them into consultation, such an outcome might be made possible. So I do not tliink it will work any hardship on the government or parliament to leave this clause over until, say to-morrow, so that we may see the amendment in Hansard and have time to study it.

subtopic: BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
Anyone who has made
i study of the conventions of the international labour office does not need to read the amendment; it is all theTe. I am not saying that the clause should not stand, but to anyone who has read article 6, this is strictly in accord with that article of the international labour office convention. I suppose the government feels it is necessary to make the clause read in that way. Article 6 reads:
Regulations made by public authority shall determine for industrial undertakings:
(b) The temporary exceptions that may be allowed, so that establishments may deal with exceptional cases of pressure of work.
These regulations shall be made only after consultation with the organizations of employers and workers concerned, if any such organizations exist. These regulations shall fix the maximum of additional hours in each instance, and the rate of pay for overtime shall not be less than one and one-quarter times the regular rate.
As I understand the amendments as they were read, they were more or less in conformity with article 6 of the convention. If many men who work overtime in industrial organizations are granted -time and a quarter by the laws of this country, this will -put a great deal of money into the pockets of our workers.

That may be quite
true. The clause covers compensation to workers. Notwithstanding opinions to the contrary, I have always held that the workers must organize in order to secure the full fruits of legislation on their behalf, and I have said this many times: If you think by giving three cheers and dropping a ballot in the box, your troubles are all over, you are just fooling yourself.

speechtext: Wait until after the election is over.

subtopic: BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext: I am not talking about bed time stories; I am talking about practical things. In Great Britain and other European countries where labour organizations are powerful, naturally they had a great deal to do with drawing up these conventions which are all predicated upon the views of the workers themselves. If this legislation in its practical application gives an impetus to the organization of workers so that they can meet their employers-and I am not one- of those who think employers and employees cannot sit down together and iron out their difficulties, because I have had some experience and I believe they can-the amendment will be a really constructive effort and will aid in bringing employees and employers together.

subtopic: BILL TO LIMIT HOURS OF WORK IN INDUSTRIAL UNDERTAKINGS
speechtext:
The amendment may be all that the hon. member for East Hamilton says, but we do not know. I defy anyone to hear it read twice and be able to decide accurately whether it covers any particular industry or branch of such; not- even a clever lawyer, let alone the average layman could do that. So far as I can judge the redrafted clause without having an opportunity to study it carefully, meets a good deal of the objections I raised the other day. As regards its application to the operation of canneries and fish plants, I should like to study it further.
Another point is this: there is an attempt to make it almost too comprehensive. It is sometimes a mistake to try to cover almost everything that can possibly arise, for when you finish you will find that you have left out the one thing you should have provided for. It is like a will. A man plans everything for his children and grandchildren, leaving out a provision for the very thing that does happen and that he could not foresee. I sent over to the minister a copy of the provision in the British Columbia laiw which has been in existence for eleven years, and which so' far as I know, has not produced any friction.

Eight Hour Day
It has the merit of being simple and I believe comprehensive also, but I suppose it would be too simple for the man who drafted this bill.
I want to make this one other point: I know the minister has had telegrams, because I have had copies of them, from the British Columbia Canners and pilchard men who protest very strongly at the idea of their being under this legislation. They point out, as the minister knows, that obviously their industry is highly seasonal and the commodity very perishable, subject to weather variations which no one can foresee and various other conditions of that kind. That is quite true. What they ask is, not that they shall have an opportunity of making representations and coming under the somewhat involved and uncertain procedure of the proposed clause 10, but to be exempted altogether under clause 2. In some industries near the border line, it might well be a matter of debate whether they should or should not be exempted, and in these cases I freely admit that it is for the minister or the governor in council to exercise judgment. But in this case there is no doubt; no one can say that there is any doubt that the fishing industry cannot be run on an eight hour day basis. It would be equally absurd to put the agricultural industry on an eight hour day and say that you can get out under clause 10. That clause states among other things that you have to consult organizations of employers and employees. In many of these industries there are not organizations or what would be considered by the government as organizations. Would it be half a dozen men in the particular factory or plant or some organization calling itself some kind of a union in British Columbia, with probably no interest at all in the merits of that particular industry? The clause also states that the maximum additional hours shall be fixed. Supposing there is a big run of fish coming in, have they to apply to Ottawa and say that suoh and such conditions prevail at this plant in this district; that under the weather conditions they could not get in with their fish yesterday and there is a heavy run today? Have they to apply to Ottawa, because the clause speaks of the power of the governor in council, to fix additional hours-and of course you can do anything if you take long enough to do it? But they cannot be fixed in that way and a business cannot be run by applying to Ottawa three thousand miles away. Here is a condition that prevails on Thursday and when they ask for relief, the reply comes back the following Tuesday. For instance, there is a steel plant with an excess of orders; that would be an unusual condition, but everyone present knows and, still more, everybody connected with the fishing business knows you cannot run it on an eight hour day basis. Then why play with the subject? Why suggest that it can ;be so run? Why not give them now the exemption which must be granted eventually? Otherwise delay is caused, and delay in the fish business means money and a great deal of it, because once the fish gets past its best, there is a heavy loss. Away out in some remote place where there is not even a radio service, they have to apply to Ottawa for an additional number of hours which may vary to-day from those of last week. It is on those grounds that the cannery men and the fish reduction plants ask that their exemption shall be definitely provided for in the bill, so that they may not have to trust to the, so to speak, day to day application. Of course it says "permanent exemption" but further on it say "wherever it is practicable the maximum of additional hours shall be fixed...." Can you fix them weeks or months ahead? It would have to be done day by day as occasion arose. You could not say that on a certain Tuesday of next month or three months hence so many additional hours should be permitted. It is for these reasons that these men ask that they be exempted finally in the bill itself.
Mr. MaoNIiCOL: The amendment may cover t'he subject matter of one or two questions I had intended to ask, in order to get a clear conception of some phrases in sections 9 and 10, but as ll could not hear all that was read, perhaps if I ask the minister now he will answer what I have in mind.
I am concerned about the promptness with which the governor in council will reply or attend to requests from industries for the privilege of changing the schedule of hours. I can quite see circumstances that would result in serious loss as far as employment is concerned if a speedy reply were not given to such a request. I have in mind some half dozen schedules used in various groups of industries. In group No. 1 they work from 8 to 12 in the morning and from 1 to 5 in the afternoon and on Saturdays from 8 to 12 in the morning, making a forty-four hour week. Group No. 2 works from 750 to 12 in the morning and 1 to 5 in the afternoon and on Saturdays from 7.20 to 12 making a forty-eight hour week. Group No. 3 work from 8 to 12 in the morning and 1230 to 4.30 and do not work at all on Saturday, a five day week of forty hours. Group No. 4 work from 8 to 12 and 1 to 5 for five days, and on Saturday from 7 to 12 a week of forty-five hours. Group No. 5 work from 7 to 12 and
Eight Hour Day

1 to 5 and five hours on Saturdays making a fifty hour week. Group No. 6 work from 7 to 12 and 1 to 5.45 for four days, eight hours on Friday and do not work on Saturday, making a forty-seven hour five-day week.
I should like to ask a question, particularly in reflation to groups 1, 3, 4 and 5 which work from forty to forty-five hours a week. If the management of such companies or groups wish to increase their schedules to forty-eigCt hours a week will they, working less than the 48 hour schedule, have to get an order from the governor in council to do it and if so will it be possible to obtain that order promptly.
Then I have in mind one or two other conditions in connection with great industries. Section 7 does give certain relief in case of urgency, and section 9 applies to the same matter. I have in mind a company receiving a rush repair order to turn out, say a new line-shaft or to make a large gear, for the want of which, employment in the whole plant is subject to disarrangement. In shaft or gear manufacturing companies their schedules are set. At present they are running on a forty hour week. What will happen in such a case where a rush order has to be taken care of? They can	put some of	the men	towork and send the	others	home	to sleep	orto rest while others work so that operations can be continuous	until	the	repairs arefinished. I would like to know if this bill provides completely for such a case, where twenty or thirty hours or more may be consumed in making a rush repair. That will of course upset the eight hour day schedule, but. that schedule can be taken care of in the three weeks allowed under one of the other sections.	But	what	I want	to
ascertain is, would such a company have to have an order in council to expedite that work, and, if so. whether the order in council would be available forthwith. After all the objects of this bill as I see them are good and among other things are designed to give the workers more leisure time and to increase the number employed. It was said yesterday that this bill would not result in any increase in the numbers employed through a reduction of working time. But anyone who has served in industry a long time knows that the reduction in hours will increase employment; perhaps not in plants in which the machines are of such a nature that they can be speeded up, but certainly in plants in which precision is the main factor the numbers to be employed will be increased.
I have in mind another case, a very recent one, in which a company was asked to produce a large order of motor engine units com-

plete. The competitor of the Canadian company was a company in Dayton, Ohio, and the company had to make up its mind quickly, 'because the delivery schedules were fairly large. During December they were to turn out twenty-five engines a day, then in . January up to the 15th they were to produce one hundred and fifty a day, and after January 15 the number was to be one hundred and eighty-five a day. But every hon. member knows that .motor car sales have increased tremendously of late, and in this case the purchasing company jumped the schedule of deliveries to two hundred a day from January 1, and two hundred and fifty on the 15th and on the 18th to four hundred a day. Now men who are capable of turning out engine units are not on tap, they have to be trained. This company so as to retain the business immediately asked the Ontario labour department to permit them to extend the hours of labour and to work in preparation part time on Sundays, and the request was granted. They then proceeded to train men, and took on about one hundred that could be specially trained to mould non-ferrous engine units. The result was that for the first week they were compelled to raise their schedule up to seventy-two hours, but the second week through additional employees they were able to reduce it to sixty hours and for the third week to fifty-five hours and during the fourth week were able to get back on the schedule of forty-eight hours after having trained additional men. I would like the minister to make clear just what a company in that line of manufacture would have to do under this bill, having in mind that the principal object of such legislation is to increase the numbers employed in industry. I could give numerous examples along the same line, but perhaps one answer will cover it all.

Mr. OHiUR'CH:	I have read the proposed
amendment to section 10 and I fail to see how it improves the section. In this country there is altogether too much in the way of contracting industries outside the provisions of statutes. This amendment gives the employer and employee the right to contract themselves out of the operations of the statute. I contend that there is altogether too much law about this act. If we are going to do something practical about an eight hour day we should cease being lawyers and think of the work done in the last few months and the revelations brought out here in Ottawa by one of the select committees of the House of Commons. We should cease pussyfooting in connection with these large corporations, mergers and combines in restraint of trade in this country, that can go to whatever government is in office and have orders in council passed. I sat in opposition as a private member and I am speaking today as a private member; after all is said
and done, a private member who represents three hundred large and small industries in his riding is the connecting link between the government of the day and the electors of that riding. I represent many working people and a large number of industries, many of which are going to find the cost of operating their plants increased as a result of this legislation. The same thing applies to chain stores to whom this act will apply. In connection with drug stores, the chain drug stores will have to increase the number of their employees and, consequently, their cost of operation, while another store perhaps next door and all the small retail stores will not be affected by the act at all. The employees in that store can work twenty-four hours a day in competition with the chain store or those who have to close.
For some seven years I was a police commissioner of the city of Toronto; for some seventeen years I was a member of the city council. We had the eight hour day; when my hon. friend from Parkdale (Mr. Spence) was a member of the council, we applied the eight hour day to all city services, including the police and fire departments. For many years the police had only one day off a month; to-day they have one day off every week, and the white collar workers of the city have had a seven hour day for forty-five years and a half-holiday from noon on Saturday.
This principle of permitting individuals to contract themselves out from under the operation of particular statutes is a vicious principle. When I was in opposition I condemned government by order in council, and I have heard other members sitting on this side do the same thing. If we want to do something practical, in view of the revelations that have been made here in the special inquiry, let us either have an eight hour day or not have it. I regret that we have had to lean on the League of Nations in order to bring in this measure. In the city of Toronto we put it through in connection with the estimates. The League of Nations is all very well in its way, but it is only for those who cannot help themselves. Every time we introduce a statute in this parliament to improve the condition of the workers we are met with the same objection; hon. gentlemen opposite refer to the British North America Act and say the proposed act is ultra vires of this parliament. They are very fond of raising the constitutional question. For nine years they sat over here; they had the example of the city of Toronto before them, but they did nothing to give the workers of this country an eight hour day. The day

before yesterday the Ontario members representing maritime cities on lake Erie and lake Ontario brought a deputation before the Minister of Marine. What were they asking for? This is a class of casual labour, which is referred to in the proposed amendment; this is casual seasonal labour for the summer and may be excepted by this amendment. The shipping interests on the great lakes are the most determined opponents of this act. They treat the men on some of these boats like cattle. The members representing Ontario maritime cities know the revelations which were contained in a memorandum prepared by these gentlemen.
I should like to refer also to the oil companies, the gasoline companies, the textile industry and the tobacco industry. Those are some of the people who are evading the law. They get over the law; they just snap their fingers at this parliament. Some of our oil companies are owned by United States companies, or interlocked with them, and the way they treat many of their employees in the larger cities is a disgrace. They give them a few dollars a week, mix them up in sports a little and then work them long hours. I know some of them worked twelve and fourteen hours a day, and some even longer. In the shipping business the situation is even worse. In the summer time off the exhibition grounds we often see these sand boats out in the lake, loading sand which is taken to the cities to be used by contractors and public bodies. Many of them work on Sundays, seven days, and the employees work many hours a day. If this amendment goes through I am afraid delegations will be in Ottawa continuously, going over the head of this parliament and appealing to the governor general in council.
I do not wish to criticize this legislation too much, but as I say I am sorry we have had to lean on the League of Nations. To-day the British North America Act is not an act for the living at all; it is an act for the dead. You cannot solve any economic problem in this country so long as that act remains in force. It is the old man of the sea on the backs 'of the people of this country, and it is a millstone around the neck of this parliament. You can cure no disease in the body politic or the body economic while that act exists. Whenever we attempt to do something we are met with opposition both in this house and on the part of the provinces, and as a result we sit here day after day and accomplish nothing in the way of relieving some of our economic problems. I know that the present government are pioneers in this work. I sympathize with the govern-

ment in having to draft the act in view of the attitude that is being taken by the opposition at 'the present time, and also because of the great burdens and artificial barriers that are being placed on business to-day and which make it almost impossible for business to carry on and therefore as I say I sympathize with the government in trying to hold an even balance in connection with this act.
I think it would be far better, instead of having a bill of thirteen clauses, to have written just one clause into the criminal code to effect the purpose we have in view in this act. It need only be a simple thing, like the Lord's Day Act, the Alien Labour Act and others, and once it is written into the code it should be strictly enforced. Of course, the industry of farming should be exempted. The farmer's capital has gone and to-day he cannot make his production costs. He is in such a position that he is to be pitied and sympathized with. We should also exempt a few of the industries dealing with the products of the sea, the soil, the forest and the mine. I admit that there are some industries that should be excepted, including our great agricultural industry. But so far as industry in general is concerned there should not be one law for the rich and another law for the poor. This particular section 10 contains some eighteen or twenty subsections and the penalties which we are providing for an infraction of these subsections are just as great for the small man as for the big corporation. Persistent evaders of the law should be treated differently from the small storekeeper. I know that most stores are exempt from this legislation, but some are not, including some of the chain stores. I believe that a civilization that is based on principles such as long hours of .labour, sweat shops, and child labour is in need of immediate and drastic overhauling and should no longer be tolerated in this country.
I am sorry that the bill does not go further than it does. No doubt it is a very good bill in many respects, and it is a start in the right direction, but like the Liquor Control Act of Ontario it will no doubt be evaded. This act should have more teeth put into it to take care of these persistent evaders, and we know there are such from the evidence that has come out before one of the committees of this house in the past fifteen months. This act should be enforced by the police court, upon summary conviction, and there should be no appeal from that court's decision. It's decision should be final. Otherwise the large corporations can engage lawyers to argue along

Eight Hour Day
the lines that have been used by hon. gentlemen opposite, that this legislation is unconstitutional. I believe that if we are going to do anything in a practical way we should not have a lot of exceptions and provisos put in the statute, but rather have one simple clause inserted in the criminal code. Why, Mr. Chairman, in 1847 England adopted an act, upon the initiative of Lord Shaftesbury, dealing with the sweat shop and providing for a shorter working day, of ten hours, and now, nearly a hundred years after, the Canadian parliament is arguing about excluding some industries from the eight hour day. That act of 1847 was the first parliamentary act of Christian socialism, and it was Christian socialism based on the evangelical Wes-leyan-Oxford movement and principles, and of Shaftesbury and men of that description. Christian socialism is not a thief; it is a policeman, and we want police to enforce this act, or the large corporations will be coming to the government of the day and asking for an order in council to get their industries exempted. This act with all its provisos and exceptions will be taken advantage of by just the very people that parliament intends to have it apply to. They will find a way of evading t>he law.
The quicker we can write an eight hour day into our law for industry, the better, and it should apply to all industry. Hours of labour and the length of shifts should be reduced. 1 hope the day is not far distant when this government will adopt the five day week and a shorter working day as a trial for one year, for the thousands and thousands of its own employees. That is the only way to make more jobs for soldieTs and civilians. 1 have been a consistent supporter of this kind of legislation long before I was in this house.
I am sorry to see so many amendments being made to the statute because I do not think they are in the public interest and in the interests of a fair enforcement of this act. I believe that these large corporations I have referred to will find a way of evading the act over the head of parliament by getting an order in council passed. Some industries in Toronto and elsewhere, for instance, can come down here when parliament is not sitting and can get an order in council virtually nullifying what this parliament has done this session. What are we here for? Are the private members just a lot of proxies? We might as well have representation by proxy if that sort of thing is going to be done. Edmund Burke said that government is a practical thing, not something to please the fancy and imagination of ordinary politicians. We are sitting here and we should deal with the merits of the questions that come before us. Should we or should we not have an eight hour day, and if we are going to have an eight hour day should it apply to all industry and to department stores as well. These department stores followed the city of Toronto over early closing at noon on Saturday during July and August. They have had to reduce their hours, and did it voluntarily I may say.
They are not included under this bill because their maximum number of hours is a fair one, but I believe the day is not far distant when we shall have to have less government by order in council and more government by the high court of parliament.

In my constituency there is a situation where several mines work seven days a week, three shifts a day, and there are a number of miners working in and around these mines. The office staff including the stenographers have to work seven days a week. There are a number of conscientious objectors there, but when they object they have to do so under their breath, because any man who does not appear on Sunday loses his job on Monday. I do not want to see the employees have to face that sort of thing. I do not think there is in this legislaiton anything that does not appear in the Lord's Day Act, and if it is not to be enforced any better than that act, there is no sense in our passing it. Having worked in the mines for some years and knowing something about them, I know there are many jobs that have to be done on Sundays. The same thing applies to the roaster, the smelter and the mill. The furnaces have to be kept white hot; there have to be men there on Sundays, but while I

speechtext:
Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 32, respecting the additional protocol of 1935 to the Canada-France trade agreement of 1933.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.

maintopic: CANADA-FRANCE TRADE AGREEMENT BILL TO CONFIBM ADDITIONAL PROTOCOL OF 1935 TO THE CONVENTION OF 1933
speechtext:
I intended on the second reading to make a general statement concerning the bill and the tariff item involved so that when it comes before the committee of the whole house hon. members may have a general view of all the provisions. For that purpose I should like to make a statement.
The house will remember that in the session of 1933 I introduced a bill to this house to confirm a commercial arrangement between Canada and France which was signed at Ottawa on May 12, 1933. I had the honour to negotiate at Paris with representatives of the government of France the provisions of that agreement which was confirmed by act of this parliament in the session of 1933. In negotiating that commercial arrangement, between the two countries, I was under certain disadvantages, due to the fact that the negotiations, opened as early as October, 1932, were begun with the government of Mr. Briand, that after the fall of that government I had to initiate the negotiations again with the government of Mr. Paul Boncour, and after that government had fallen I had to resume negotiations with the government of Mr. Deladier, which were postponed until a French commission came to Washington and I had an opportunity to continue negotiations at New York with that commission and at Ottawa with Mr. Arsene Henry the French Minister to Canada in respect of the matters which had been left unfinished in the negotiations at Paris.
In the negotiations at Paris the government of France naturally contended for more favourable terms of admission for French brandies, liqueurs and wines into Canada.

Difficulties then occurred arising out of the empire trade agreements made at the imperial conference which had recently been held at Ottawa, because under the agreements then made with South Africa and Australia their wines were given certain preferential treatment, and, under the agreement with the United Kingdom made at that conference, brandies from the United Kingdom had preferential treatment on entry into Canada. After the agreement with France was signed at Ottawa on May 12, 1933, negotiations were reopened between the government of Canada and the government of France through Mr. Arsene Henry the French minister, with regard to more favourable terms of admission for French wines, liqueurs and brandies than were agreed upon in the convention of May 12, 1933. It was therefore necessary for the government of Canada to open negotiations with the government of South Africa and also the government of Australia on the one hand, and with the government of the United Kingdom on the other, before the concession which France then sought could be granted by Canada. Those negotiations proceeded until Mr. Arsene Henry left Canada with certain propositions which were to be placed before the government of France for consideration. Later the Prime Minister of Canada and the Under Secretary of State for External Affairs visited Geneva as representatives of Canada at the Geneva assembly of September, 1934, and on their return from Geneva a protocol forming a supplementary trade agreement between Canada and France was drawn up and signed in Paris by the Prime Minister on September 19, 1934. That new agreement conceded more favourable terms of entry to Canada on French wines, liqueurs and brandies, and it came into force by reason of a provision in the Tariff Act which enables the government of Canada by order in council to make concessions to a foreign country in consideration of equivalent concessions being made in the tariff of the foreign country with respect to importations into that country of Canadian goods.
The present bill is intituled an act rsepect-ing the additional protocol of 1935 to the Canada-France trade agreement of 1932. The term "protocol" is one employed, I believe, in diplomatic practice to denote an agreement, somewhat less formal than a convention and which usually revises or modifies an earlier treaty or convention. In the present case the draftsman of the bill has deemed it desirable to use the term "additional protocol" rather than the simple term "protocol"

Canada-France Agreement
in order to distinguish between the protocol as expressed in the arrangement which is annexed to the bill and confirmed by the bill and the notes signed at Paris by the Prime Minister on September 29, 1934, which were published in the Commercial Intelligence Journal issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce dated October 6, 1934, and are therefore quite well known in all commercial circles in Canada. But since those notes were signed and delivered in Paris certain other concessions have been made on both sides, so that the agreement which is now before the house for ratification by this bill embodies not only the concessions made by the notes of September 29, 1934, signed at Paris, but also additional concessions which have been negotiated since that time between our Department of External Affairs and the French government through the present French minister to Canada.
When the notes were signed in Paris it was contemplated that these further negotiations would take place, and therefore when certain other concessions were made by both parties they were embodied in the additional protocol which forms the schedule to this bill.
Certain difficulties had arisen with regard to carrying into full effect the commercial treaty of May, 1933. On June 16, 1934, Canadian wheat had become dutiable under the French general tariff, and the French exchange compensation surtax and the special import tax levied by France were detrimental to the improvement of Canadian trade with that country, the export of Canadian wheat and flour to France in particular being prejudicially affected. The first tariff reductions which were made upon the exchange of notes in September, 1934, were embodied and made effective by order in council P.C. 2420 under section 11 of the customs tariff, which provides that the governor general in council may by order in council make such reductions of duties on goods imported into Canada from any other country or countries as may be deemed reasonable by way of compensation for reductions on Canadian products imported by any such country or countries. If the house so desires I will see that at the conclusion of my remarks a copy of that order in council is laid upon the table
of the house for the information of hon. members.
After that exchange of notes the French government by administrative decree extended the benefits of their minimum tariff to a considerable list of Canadian products and accorded definite quotas on a number of Canadian products of classes subject to quota. The French government also reduced the special import tax and cancelled the exchange compensation surtax so far as Canadian goods were concerned. To make that clear may I state that after we had negotiated the convention with France of May 11, 1933, by which our exports to France were admitted under the minimum tariff, the French government undertook to limit exports from Canada to that country, while admitting them under their minimum tariff, by prescribing quotas by which our exports were restricted to certain quantities and certain times. Under the convention of May, 1933, two quotas were recognized, one on lobsters and the other on salmon products. Thereafter, however, due to the difficulties which the French government met in maintaining their currency on a gold standard, they felt impelled to restrict their importations from foreign countries, and they proceeded to make global quotas which restricted to certain quantities the entire imports into France from foreign countries, allotting to Canada a certain percentage of those global quotas. So although our products continued to be admitted under the minimum tariff of France the quantities which could be so admitted were restricted by their quota policy.
I would direct the attention of hon. members to schedule C of the protocol now under consideration. The additional protocol was mainly designed to extend tariff concessions on both sides to cover commodities which it was not found possible to investigate fully in the September negotiations, and if hon. members will allow me I will call attention to those additional concessions. Would it be necessary for me to read them or might I be allowed to place them on the record?

If the hon. member has been following the schedule C he will see that the rates are being reduced. Perhaps I might give the explanation which will have to be given sooner or later. The difficulty in connection with the importation of French products is the fact that the prices in Canada seem to be high is due to the rate of exchange between Canadian and French currencies. France has remained on the gold standard while at the present time in international exchange we find that our currency in terms of gold has depreciated by about forty per cent. The result is that the Canadian dollar expressed in terms of gold now represents about sixty cents in gold of the old standard. It sometimes runs around fifty-nine cents but I am taking sixty cents as the average. The result is that the French product which we formerly bought and paid for with a dollar of our currency by the purchase of exchange on France is now bought and paid for with our currency computed at a depreciation of forty per cent. What I bought before at a certain price in French francs now requires sixty-six and two-thirds more in Canadian currency to pay for the same product bought at the same price in francs in France. I had this brought home to me when my wife told me that she was making some purchases of toilet and dress articles in France. She said the price in French francs was exactly the same, but when she paid for them in Canadian currency she found that the price in Canadian currency had increased as forty is to sixty, that is, by two-thirds, which is sixty-six and two-thirds per cent. So that those of us who occasionally purchase French wines may not hope, despite the present reduction in the tariff on French wines, to purchase French wines in Canada at the same low price expressed in Canadian currency as we did before the fall in the value of the Canadian dollar in international exchange.

The natural or manufactured products, originating in and coming from Canada, enumerated
Canada-France Agreement

in supplementary schedule A to this additional protocol, and the natural or manufactured products, originating in and coming from French customs territory, enumerated in supplemenl ary schedule C to this additional protocol, shall, on their importation into the territory of the other party, enjoy the most favourable rates accorded to any foreign country, that may arise from modifications made in the tariff classification as a result of administrative or legislative action or of conventions entered into with other countries.
The result is that, in respect of these schedules, if France makes any larger concessions by way of reducing her tariff in favour of any other foreign country Canada will enjoy the advantage of these concessions; and if Canada, in negotiations with any other foreign country, grants a lower rate of duty to any such foreign country, these reduced rates automatically apply to French products.
In article 4 the same reductions apply with respect to the French colonies and it is provided that:
The natural or manufactured products, originating inland coming from French colonies, "assimilees" and "non-assimilees," countries under French protectorate, and territories under French mandate, enumerated in supplementary schedule (C) to this additional protocol shall enjoy any other more favourable tariff rate which Canada may accord' to the same or simiar products of any other foreign country.

Article 7 of the additional protocol is one of the most important for Canada, and I shall read it in full:
Article 7
In the event that the system of temporary admission of wheat into France is modified or abandoned, and that suitable facilities are not provided whereby wheat, the produce of Canada, would' retain marketing opportunities in France equivalent to those now enjoyed, the French government recognize the right of the Canadian government, with regard to the advantages conceded by the present additional protocol in respect of wines, liqueurs, cognac and Armagnac, specified in supplementary schedule C to this additional protocol, to take whatever measures they may consider advisable, provided that these measures shall not constitute a discrimination against France as compared with any other foreign country.
Since December 1, 1929, there has been in France a domestic milling quota which as at present applied makes it compulsory, subject to certain provisions to which I shall hereafter refer, to use one hundred per cent of French domestic wheat in wheat flour produced in France for home consumption. Due
to this regulation, Canadian wheat except when admitted under the "temporary admission' system to which this article 7 refers, may be imported into France for purposes other than human food, such as seeding, animal feed, industrial use, et cetera, in which cases a special licence must be obtained by the importer and the wheat must be thoroughly denatured by colouring at the customs port of entry. There has been practically no demand in France for denatured foreign wheat, as the domestic product has filled all the requirements of that market, and therefore for practical purposes the result is that all Canadian wheat imported into France has to enter under the "temporary admission" system.
The French "temporary admission" system permits the refund of customs duties paid on importations of foreign wheat, upon the exportation by the French miller of a corresponding quantity of French wheat in the form of flour. For instance, a French miller imports 1,000 bushels of Canadian wheat under a "temporary admission" permit, and he deposits or is debited under this arrangement
Canada-Fmnce Agreement

with the amount of the customs duties on the wheat which he has imported into France. If thereafter, within a maximum delay determined by the law, the miller exports a corresponding quantity of French flour, the amount of the import duty deposited in respect of the importation of foreign wheat is refunded or credited to the miller in France by the customs authorities. This privilege of exporting domestic flour to compensate for importations of foreign wheat was granted at the request of the. French millers, who have claimed and continue to claim that a certain proportion of foreign wheat must be blended with French wheat to obtain certain grades of flour which are required in France for domestic use. Foreign wheat so imported is of a class corresponding to our hard wheat in Alberta and Saskatchewan, which is not produced in France. Hon. gentlemen will remember that on a previous occasion I drew the attention of the house to the fact that France in the very year I think in which I negotiated the treaty of May, 1933, produced within its own country more wheat than was produced in all Canada, but they did not produce in France proper the equivalent of Canadian hard wheat. They have, as I pointed out to the house on a previous occasion, been importing Saskatchewan wheat and planting it in colonies of northern Africa which belong to France. They found in the first year that from Saskatchewan seed they produced a hard wheat; planting then as seed again their own product, they produced a very good hard wheat in the second year; but I was told that in the third year the wheat so produced begins to lose its quality of hardness and to become a soft wheat which is not as good for mixing for domestic use in France. The foreign wheat imported into France under the "temporary admission" system becomes according to French law "nationalized"; that is, legally assimilated to French wheat, and may be mixed with French wheat in any proportion for milling purposes regardless of the quota.
The concession afforded to Canada on wheat, namely the French minimum tariff, was undoubtedly a valuable one to this country, and from the Canadian point of view it was very important that the principle of this "admission temporaire" should not be abolished in respect of Canada. That became the subject of these later negotiations. From the French point of view the concessions accorded on 
French cognac, and liqueurs and sparkling and non-sparkling wines, our Canadian tariff items Ex 156, Ex 163 and Ex 165, were also important for the extension of the French wine trade in Canada, and so in this additional protocol it was agreed to make the Canadian tariff concessions on French cognac and liqueurs and sparkling and non-sparkling wines conditional upon the maintenance by France of facilities under which Canadian wheat would retain its present marketing opportunities in France. That is the purpose of article 7 which I have just read, and which in the view of the government establishes a very important principle.
Article 8 deals with another matter. It reads:
The increase in the rate of the import tax provided' by article 32 of the law of March 31, 1932, shall not apply, as long as the present additional protocol remains in force, to products originating in Canada, in accordance with the terms of the decree of September 29, 1934.
The application of the French special import tax of four per cent on semi-manufactured goods and six per cent on manufactured goods affected detrimentally our competitive position in the French market. When I had the honour to negotiate in France on behalf of the Canadian government for the trade agreement of May, 1933, I urged very strongly that these special import taxes of four and six per cent should be removed or reduced. I was unable at that time to obtain an agreement to that effect, but the French government gave assurances that they would give favourable consideration to the Canadian representations, but it was then claimed that it was impracticable to remove these import taxes at once, since manufactured products of French origin had to bear at various stages of manufacture a turnover tax of two per cent, and were therefore at a disadvantage compared with imported foreign goods which paid an import tax at uniform rate of two per cent regardless of their degree of manufacture. In view, however, of the concessions which have been made to other countries Canada pressed for equal treatment with the United Kingdom, Belgium and Italy, which had been accorded a rate of two per cent. The effect of this article 8 is to afford to Canadian goods the rate of two per cent instead of four and six per cent respectively which had formerly been imposed, and thus places Canadian goods

on a footing of equality with those of the most favoured nations in this respect.
Article 9 deals with maple sugar and maple products. The trade agreement signed on May 12, 1933, conceded to Canada minimum tariff rates on maple sugar and maple syrup. The effect of article 9 in this additional protocol is to secure a further concession by exempting maple sugar and maple syrup, when imported for use in the manufacture of tobacco, from certain internal taxes which are levied on sugar in France. The main internal tax, which is now cancelled, is a consumption tax of 85 francs per one hundred kilograms, about 2J cents per pound at the present rate of exchange. A refining tax of 2 francs, and a surveillance tax of \ franc per one hundred kilograms are also cancelled but taxes levied internally in France will nevertheless apply to maple sugar and maple syrup if imported for uses other than in the preparation of French tobacco.
The French decree of December 5, 1931, mentioned in article 9, authorized the government to limit by quota the importations of foreign sugar, and the other decree mentioned, that of October 8, 1934, limited to 32,000 metric tons the quantity of foreign sugar that could be imported in the period between October 8, 1934, and October 15, 1935. Article 9 exempts Canadian maple sugar and maple syrup imported for use in the preparation of tobacco from these quota restrictions. If maple sugar and maple syrup are imported from Canada into France for any other purpose there is an annual quota fixed for Canada of 1,000 kilograms or one metric ton.
As to article 10, on certain articles of clothing for children, by order in council No. 2838 of November 12, 1931, the price was fixed at S8 and S9 per dozen. The French government contended that the values so fixed under the authority of that order in council were much in excess of the true market value of the articles, and it was accordingly agreed to reduce the value for duty under section 43 of the Customs Act to 84.50 per dozen, or about one-half. With respect to cherries "glace" the value for duty had been fixed by the Department of National Revenue at 8 francs per kilogram, and the French government contended that the market price in France did not exceed 6-5 francs per kilogram, and it was accordingly
agreed to reduce the value for duty by twenty per cent.
Little need be said by me with respect to the remaining articles 11, 12 and 13. A feature of the negotiations which, though not set forth in the articles of agreement, will result in considerable advantage to Canada is the cancellation of the exchange compensation surtax on Canadian goods. By a French decree of November 12, 1931, the French government imposed an exchange compensation surtax ranging from seven to twenty-five per cent ad valorem on imports from. specified countries whose currencies were then depreciated as compared with the French franc. It was stated that the purpose of these surtaxes was to countervail the indirect exchange bounty resulting from the depreciation of certain foreign currencies from their legal parity. Articles which are exempt from French customs duty under the French minimum tariff, such as wheat, for which a world market exists, are not subject to this surtax in France. On December 10, 1931, an exchange compensation surtax at the rate of eleven per cent ad valorem was imposed on all goods imported from Canada. Canada's competitive position in the French market was thereby rendered more difficult. In 1934 the French government cancelled the exchange compensation surtax on goods imported from the United Kingdom, the Irish Free State, Norway, Finland and the U.SS.R. Now, as the result of this exchange of notes, the French government has exempted all imports from Canada from the operation of this exchange compensation surtax, placing , Canadian goods in a better competitive position in the French market.

Let them follow the principles of Gladstone, of Disraeli, of Campbell-Bannerman, of Baldwin, of Blake, of George Brown, of Laurier, of Borden, of all those great political men who have written history. Let the minister have an opportunity to consult his assistant so as to be able to answer the question intelligently.
Carried.
If you have no more respect for the minister than that, he ought to get out of your company and resign.
The hon. member for Gloucester knows French well enough-

The hon. member has insinuated something to that effect and I want to answer the charge.

Were there any supercharge raised stamps, from five to six cents, of the air mail, sold to stamp collectors or vendors or purchasers, whatever the minister likes to call them? I do not think that we
should be required to place a question of that kind on the order paper. The Postmaster General's estimates are now before the committee and he can answer the question. I do not want to push him to-night, but so long as that -answer is not given I dfc not think that these estimates should pass. That is the point I make. The Postmaster General, speaking in French, said that I was not treating him right. I have sat on this side for four sessions and have listened to the minister's estimates going through. master General's estimates, not only in a general way but in detail, and when the hon. gentleman, reviewing my attitude in the last four years, can get up and say that I am not treating him right because I want a definite answer to a question which interests the public as a whole concerning what to my mind is one of the worst principles ever established in the Post Office Department, namely, allowing outsiders to make a profit on the sale of stamps which should go to the government, then I say that he cannot appreciate it when he is properly treated, and from now on I will reserve to myself the right to criticize him as severely as I feel he should be criticized. I have not criticized the Postmaster General; I have endeavoured to have his estimates go through. I know the responsibility that rests upon his shoulders; I know what a difficult department he has to administer; I know that he represents the largest vending and revenue department of the government of Canada; I know that he has from thirty-five to forty thousand men under his supervision, and I know how difficult it is to administer the department without having undue criticism hurled at him. For this reason I have refrained from criticizing the minister. But when it came to my notice within the last day or two that this transaction was put through in 1932, I felt it my duty not to criticize the minister severely but simply to point out that this had been done and to find out the reasons why it had been done and why outside parties should have been allowed to participate in the surplus revenue that should have come to the Post Office Department. I think the minister has gone out of his way to-night in stating that I have treated him unfairly in handling the question. When I was Postmaster General I stood here for twenty-one days with my estimates held up, but I found no fault with the opposition for the action they took because I was able to meet them. I was able to answer every question that was put to me; I was able to meet and answer every attack that was hurled against me; I stood by my guns and I refused to give in even when the opposition in the dying hours of the attack, after twenty-one days, thought I could no longer go across to England and sit as the first Canadian who ever sat as president of the world postal union, and when they offered to compromise and withdraw their dogs I refused to accept the compromise. If I were to show toward the minister the same disposition that his friends displayed towards me during my tenure of office, he would never get his estimates through the house.
All right; go ahead.

What have you to say about the matter? You are not the minister and you know very little about what is going on in the house. Pardon me, Mr. Chairman, for addressing the hon. gentleman directly and not through the chair, but he had no right to interfere. The biblical injunction is that when you are struck on one cheek, you should turn the other. I want to say that I newer turned the other cheek, but I fought straight from the shoulder. I have every sympathy for the Postmaster General. I know his department is not allowed to be run to-day in the way it should be run; I know he is not the master of that department. In my time I would brook no interference in the internal working of the department from any member of the government, not even from the Prime Minister under whom I worked. He knew enough, in carrying on the business of the country, to allot to each minister his department and to rely upon each minister to be able to conduct it properly. That is not the situation to-day, and proof of that is to be found in the fact that for the last two years there has been no deputy postmaster general. Why? If rumour that is circulating is true, the position is being kept vacant for the appointment of a Conservative member of this house who fears that he will not be elected in his constituency in the next election.
Name him. '

No; hon. gentlemen opposite can name him better than I can, because some of them, as I understand the matter, have been pushing his application to the fore. There is just now a little row in the Conservative party to see which one of two or three should get the position, and not one of those gentlemen whose names are mentioned is fit to fill the position of assistant deputy or assistant to the assistant deputy of the Post Office Department, because they do not know the first thing about it. I want to appeal now to the government: Name your deputy minister according to merit; do not go outside the department and take in to place at the head of that important department a man who knows nothing about it. Name a man according to merit; such men are to be found in the Post Office Department. There are in it members of the civil service the equal of whom cannot be found on the whole continent of America, and I say that after having had four years experience with such men. There are in that department men the equal of whom cannot be found in any other

civil service on this continent; there are there men whom the United' States and France take the trouble to consult in regard to the method of administering their departments of mail service. Let me appeal once more to the government: Grant to the service the money that it deserves; do not hold that position open any longer. I say to the government of to-day: Should the fortunes of war in the coming election go against them and your humble servant is called upon to fill the position he once filled in the government of another day, if a deputy minister is appointed from outside the service, I will cut his head off five minutes after I take office.
Why?
Political patronage.

It is not a question of political patronage; it is a question of fitness for the position, because if you appoint a man from outside the civil service he would ruin and wreck that department inside of three months. That is why I stand by the principle of promotion. I want promotion in the service. I carried out that principle when I was at the head of the Post Office Department, and I want the present government to carry it out and to appoint men from within the service and not to give such positions to political heelers.

I do not wish to derogate from the glory of the former Postmaster General. I notice he has a beautiful rose in the lapel of his coat and I think all that is needed now is a laurel wreath to deck his brow. ities very much in need of new post offices. What are the factors that enter into the establishment of new offices? How many miles apart must they be? conditions and needs.

Last year I drew the minister's attention to the fact that some sixty householders in a 'district within a mile of the post office at New Westminster who have no mail delivery had to put up boxes seven or eight blocks away, although the district all round them is served with a house to house delivery. I am making an appeal this year on behalf of those householders. Surely if the district surrounding them can be given a house to house delivery there is no reason why this district should not have it. There are about sixty householders and the district is growing fast. I know the statement has been made that before there can be house to house delivery there must be sidewalks. It may be true that sidewalks should be constructed in low lying districts, but the district of which I am speaking is one of the highest areas in the town,, and if it rained forty days and forty nights one could still walk with dry feet there because it is not only on a hill but is also very gravelly. I see an increase in the estimates of some $9,600, and I make an earnest plea on behalf of these people. They are well within the city limits, and I do not think the excuse that it would require one extra postman should be considered sufficient for refusing a service that is long overdue. I ask the Postmaster General what can be done about it this year.
I shall have an inquiry made immediately and will inform the hon. member what it is possible to do.

Could the minister tell me why the people's own railroad, with so much more mileage, should get less than the Canadian Pacific?
The amount paid the Canadian Pacific is greater because the trains of this company operate through districts more densely populated than the districts through which the Canadian National operates.

The thought has passed through my mind, and I wondered if the government had taken it into consideration, of pooling the amounts paid the two railroads and dividing them equally between the two companies.
I do not think that would be practicable.

I have heard that question asked many times; I have asked it myself, and in addition to what my hon. friend the Postmaster General has said in regard to the density of population there is another very good reason why the Canadian Pacific happen to have more business in the carrying of mails than the Canadian National. As Minister of Railways I am naturally interested, and I am told that the Canadian Pacific, being the older system, having been the only system as a matter of fact up to 1900 or 1903, and having not only the denser traffic but also the older contracts, naturally has continued those contracts because there has been no good reason advanced for taking them away, since the contracts have been

properly carried out. I think that has a good deal to do with the fact that the Canadian Pacific has that advantage. Yet another reason is that the Canadian Pacific, with its ocean services on both Atlantic and Pacific, furnishes a through route, and naturally that must be taken into consideration to a certain extent.

May I ask the hon. minister to quit his laconism for a while and give us some details or try to justify what I consider to be an injustice which he has committed when he dismissed Hector Hudon as mail carrier in St. Pascal? After an investigation, he kept him in his position, and if I am well informed, it was during his trip to Egypt-I wouldn't call it 'his flight to Egypt-that the matter was settled to the detriment of Mr. Hudon. Upon his return I saw the hon. minister, I explained to him the facts the best I could and I was very astonished to hear, last December, that without a word of warning on his part, the contract had been taken away from Mr. Hudon, after an investigation which proved absolutely nothing. If the hon. minister would refer to his files, I think he would find a letter from Father Langlais, parish priest of St. Pascal, strongly protesting against the stand taken by the department.

I understand that it would rather be for the hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) to answer this question, because he was acting minister when the hon. minister was visiting Egypt. At any rate if the minister would give some explanation, I would be very glad, because I cannot see anything fair in this dismissal.

That is a
matter of opinion. Everything has its bright and its dark side. Some held that it was fair to leave this contract to Mr. Hudon, while others thought it was unfair. There were representations from both sides, from Mr. Hudon s friends and from his opponents. The latter were complaining about his conduct, and after having weighed the evidence, I came to the conclusion which has just been referred to by the hon member for Kamouraska (Mr. Bouchard). It is true that I received a letter from the parish priest expressing certain opinions; other people expressed different views. I Tespected them all, but finally had to make a decision myself.

Mr. Chairman, I am very glad to see the hon. solicitor general in his seat. Perhaps he remembers this case which I consider extremely unfair. The minister hesitated a long time and he states that there were reasons pro and con. I would like tc know what may have been the reasons to justify this dismissal. There are many against it, but I do not see any for which they should have dismissed Hector Hudon, a mail carrier who was doing his work quite well. They have never been able to prove anything against him in the performance of his duties. Outside of his duties he had, it is true, an automobile accident, but that has nothing to do with his contracts with the government. I even believe that the mail carriers may, outside of their work, mix in politics, without being liable to be dismissed.
This man had secured a contract for the carrying of mail and he fulfilled it very well. Absolutely nothing was proved against him, but they deprived him of a position upon which he relied for a living. He was fulfilling his task admirably. It is not a case of political partisanship. He has the support of all the citizens including the parish priest and barring none. The first time the case was brought up, I know that the hon. minister thought that the circumstances were in favour of Mr. Hudon, since he maintained him in his position. But I repeat that in the absence of the Postmaster General the acting Postmaster General who is the hon. Solicitor General
thought that he could do better, I suppose, than the Postmaster General and he ordered a new investigation. Afterwards he asked for new tenders and virtually proclaimed the dismissal of Mr. Hudon. The case was left in abeyance until the return of the Postmaster General, who, after having recovered from the fatigue of his long trip, was able to take the matter under consideration, and, finally, in December, without a word of warning and without giving anybody a chanc.e to weigh the circumstances, Hudon was dismissed. I consider that it is absolutely unfair and I challenge the minister to deny the facts at any time, on any public platform, or elsewhere. I even invite the Solicitor General, who is well known in our district, to come to St. Pascal and discuss this case before the people. I believe he will realize that never so great an injustice has been done in a county by the Post Office Department.

This
amount is required to provide for Canada's yearly contribution to the international customs tariffs bureau. We make a great deal of use of that bureau. I direct the attention of the minister to a prevalent complaint in Alberta with regard to the weighing of coal. I understand that the coal is not weighed at the pit mouth but on the cars by the railway companies, and there is complaint of shortage of weight with regard to almost every car. Inasmuch as this comes under the jurisdiction of the minister's department I should like to have him investigate the matter in order to see that the railway companies weigh the coal properly, because we are satisfied that proper precautions cannot be taken to weigh the cars and then take off the tare to determine the actual amount of coal in the car. By this method a shortage occurs, with the result that the companies who retail the coal have to sell to consumers less coal than they should. They sell a short ton instead of giving full weight in order to make up the deficiency. I am informed that the railway companies do not stop the cars on the scale but run them over the scale slowly, and this is responsible for the shortage. Will the minister take action in this regard, because the complaint is prevalent.
